 Is pop culture making annual leave planning more complex?
 Ahead of the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, People Management explores whether HR needs to update its calendar to anticipate absence
 by 
 Islam Soliman 
 18 November 2026 
 Share article on Twitter 
 Share article on Facebook 
 Share article on LinkedIn 
 Getty Images 
 From blockbuster films to video game launches, concerts to television finales, pop culture is giving employees more reasons to book time off.  
 With some workers counting down to the launch of  Grand Theft Auto VI on 19 November, annual leave bookings are already 18 per cent higher than on comparable Thursdays in 2024 and 2025, according to Breathe HR research covering more than 330,000 UK employees. 
 And gaming is not the only form of entertainment influencing holiday bookings. Separate Bright HR research found that 70,198 UK employees booked time off to watch Barbie , Oppenheimer or both when the films were released in July 2023, suggesting that major film releases can also influence annual leave patterns.

 Television releases have also prompted fans to take time off. When the second season of Netflix's Stranger Things was released in 2017, some viewers claimed to have called in sick to binge watch the show. 
 While such cultural moments may influence when employees request leave, Bharat Siyani, VP for people and culture at Breathe HR, argues that how employees spend their time off should not be a concern. 
 “Workers are entitled to take their annual leave for whatever reasons they please, and employers can only refuse a request if they give the right amount of notice and have a genuine business reason,” he explains. 
 But as pop culture increasingly influences when employees want time off, does HR need to become more culturally aware of the events that matter to its workforce? 
 ‘The HR calendar used to be simple’ 
 Siyani says employers need to broaden their approach to annual leave planning to reflect the growing influence of pop culture. “The HR calendar used to be simple: Christmas, bank holidays and the odd World Cup. Not anymore. For many younger workers, a major game launch matters as much as a cup final,” he adds. “For businesses, the lesson is to look ahead.” 
 However, Emma Cromarty, director at consultancy EC Human Resources, says HR does not need to become a “culture calendar”, but should instead identify events that could have a meaningful impact on staffing. 
 Siyani adds: “That way there’s no nasty surprises and you can say yes to requests while keeping business running smoothly.” 
 The question, then, is not whether HR should keep track of every major release or celebration, but how employers can spot potential “pinch points” early enough to respond, Cromarty says. 
 ‘Little excuse to remain reactive’ 
 Daniel Moczynski, head of HR at recycling and waste management business The NWH Group, argues that there is “little excuse to remain reactive” when employers already have access to information that could help them anticipate demand. 
 “Patterns in annual leave, absence and workforce demand can tell us a great deal,” he says.  
 For Siyani, conversations with employees can make a difference. “HR leaders should keep an eye on what matters to their teams and talk openly about the big cultural moments on the horizon. That way, they can plan cover ahead of time rather than being caught short on the day,” he says. 
 Yet identifying demand is only part of the challenge, Siyani continues. Employers must also decide how to maintain staffing levels when several people want the same day off. 
 Gary Cookson, director of consultancy Epic HR, suggests agreeing minimum staffing levels in advance, alongside practical measures such as cross-training employees, arranging temporary cover or rescheduling less urgent work. 
 However, Moczynski stresses that workforce planning should not fall entirely on HR, with operational leaders also needing to understand the factors influencing employees’ availability. 
 “HR plays an important role in providing insight and challenging assumptions, but operational leaders must own workforce planning,” he says. “It cannot become HR’s problem every time several colleagues request the same day off.” 
 Even with these arrangements in place, some employers may still have to turn down requests, adds Moczynski. And that raises a more difficult question: how should managers decide whose leave takes priority? 
 Cromarty says businesses should explore flexible arrangements where possible and communicate decisions clearly, avoiding situations where individual managers make inconsistent judgements. 
 “The aim should be transparency and consistency, so employees understand the rules and managers aren’t making ad-hoc decisions under pressure,” she explains. 
 Moczynski warns that a blanket first-come, first-served system might be “administratively convenient” but does not automatically make it fair. 
 Cookson agrees that employers need to look beyond the order in which requests arrive and consider the individual circumstances involved. “The real test of fairness isn’t whether everyone gets the same answer. It’s whether everyone gets a decision that takes their circumstances seriously.”
